newsitem.title: USA: Phelps Dodge sells options to raise cash.
newsitem.headline: Phelps Dodge sells options to raise cash.

text.p: Phelps Dodge Corp has joined a growing line of U.S. copper producers who have sold some of their put options to raise cash to cushion their bottom lines following the post-Sumitomo plunge in red metal prices.
"It just boils down to the bird in the hand versus the unknown possibility of experiencing some proceeds in the future," said Phelps' chief financial officer, Thomas St. Clair.

On Monday Phelps said in a statement that 95 million pounds, or half of its fourth quarter contracts, have been sold for $8.8 million, and 85 million pounds, or half of the first quarter 1997 contracts, have been sold for $6.8 million.

The related gains will be deferred and recognised in income during the periods to which the original contracts were applicable. Put options are bought by producers to guard against metal prices falling.
"They are just taking some profits, viewing it as an opportunity to lock in something that will be good for their bottom line," said Merrill Lynch analyst William O'Neill.
Only a quarter of Phelps's 350 to 400 million pound quarterly production is now covered by put options compared to a half before.
No alternative price risk management has been undertaken.
"The easy answer, which we have not done and don't plan to do, is to sell forward on LME or to a buyer," St. Clair said. "We just sell priced at the time of shipment."

St. Clair suggested the sale indicated that Phelps took a bullish view on prices - the puts were in the 90 to 95 cents per pound range. Benchmark December COMEX copper settled at 87.90 cents per pound Tuesday, up 1.30 cents.

"If we thought that the market was likely to go south from those levels, then our decision would be to hold the options," St. Clair said. "Our view is the likelihood is that the market is not going to be terrifically strong, but it's not likely to go significantly weaker either."

In August Freeport McMoRan Copper & Gold Inc sold additional copper put options and now has no price protection. ASARCO said in July it sold some of its put options to reap extra pre-tax profits of $35 million.
Some banks are said by copper industry sources to have had their fingers burnt by selling the put options to producers before red metal prices plunged low enough to bring them into play.

On Wednesday the U.S. House of Representatives committee on banking and financial services will hold a hearing on the Sumitomo scandal, exploring the extent of U.S. bank involvement, among other issues.
St. Clair declined to name who sold Phelps the options, other than "financial institutions", but admitted that the Sumitomo debacle has made put options much more expensive.
"The availability of put options has been materially reduced as a result of the changes since June as a result of the Sumitomo situation," St. Clair said.
The outlook for the third quarter was "pretty good. Copper is strong in terms of quantity but the price is weaker than it was in the prior period," St. Clair said.
Sales to the building industry and telecommunications continued to be strong with the outlook remaining good into the fourth quarter, St. Clair added.
